# Decision log — constant-checking

## [#1] 2026-09-30 · DISCOVERY · 5 Research Setting
Element 5 reports a sample drawn mainly from the authors' own personal and professional networks, supplemented by Mechanical Turk; element 8's contribution claims and element 9's boundary discussion do not name this convenience-recruitment as a limit on generalizability, even though theoretical sampling explicitly does not aim at a representative population. [tentative, src: gerlach-cenfetelli-2020 p. 1709; 1721]

## [#2] 2026-09-30 · DISCOVERY · 9 Boundary Conditions and Limitations
The cultural and legal boundary of the theory (element 9.1) is argued only through the sample's composition — Europe and the United States — and a passing citation of WHO/APA classification practice; the paper never states outright that its causal account (need to stay up to date, enduring goals) was only tested within societies of comparably high, unrestricted IT accessibility. [tentative, src: gerlach-cenfetelli-2020 p. 1707; 1721-1722]

## [#3] 2026-09-30 · DISCOVERY · 4 Theoretical Constructs and Relationships
Element 4's theorizing rests on separating habitual from deliberate checking (7.2's counter-instances), but no criterion in element 6's design or analysis distinguishes the two beyond the researchers' own coding judgment and participants' retrospective self-labeling; the boundary between the two is asserted rather than operationalized. [tentative, src: gerlach-cenfetelli-2020 p. 1712-1713]

## [#4] 2026-09-30 · DISCOVERY · 6 Research Design and Analysis
Element 6.3's rebuttal to self-report and social-desirability concerns — that participants were "generally very self-critical" and readily admitted checking in inappropriate situations — is itself drawn from the same self-report data the concern is about; nothing external to the interviews and surveys corroborates that participants were not still under-reporting. [tentative, src: gerlach-cenfetelli-2020 p. 1721]

## [#5] 2026-09-30 · DISCOVERY · 3 Research Question
RQ3 in element 3.1 asks when checking leads to "positive or negative outcomes," but element 7's findings and Figure 1 instead frame outcomes as "intended" versus "unintended." The paper itself notes it refrains from labeling outcomes positive or negative, so the research question and the reported findings answer the same puzzle in two different vocabularies that are never explicitly reconciled. [tentative, src: gerlach-cenfetelli-2020 p. 1706; 1717]
